content:
# Baruch Chapter 4 — Disagreement Log

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Chapter:** Baruch 4 (37 verses)
**Agents:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Total Disagreements:** 18

---

## Disagreement 001 — v.2: "Turn, O Jacob" vs. "Turn back, O Jacob" vs. "Come back, Jacob"

**EMET:** "Turn, O Jacob, and take hold of her"
**LOGOS:** "Turn back, O Jacob, and take hold of her"
**PNEUMA:** "Come back, Jacob"
**Issue:** Greek epistraphēti = turn/turn back (imperative of epistrephō). The verb implies repentance/return. LOGOS "turn back" is most idiomatic. PNEUMA "come back" loses the directional specificity (turning toward Wisdom). Consensus: "Turn back, O Jacob."

---

## Disagreement 002 — v.2: "light" and "brightness" / "radiance" / "fires"

**EMET:** "walk toward her light, toward the brightness of her fires"
**LOGOS:** "walk toward her light, toward the radiance of her fires"
**PNEUMA:** "Walk toward her light, toward the brightness of her flames"
**Issue:** Greek lampros = brightness/radiance. "Radiance" (LOGOS) is slightly more elevated. "Flames" (PNEUMA) vs. "fires" (EMET) — Greek pyros = fire/fires. Consensus: "toward the radiance of her fires."

---

## Disagreement 003 — v.3: "advantages" vs. "blessings" vs. "gifts"

**EMET:** "your advantages to a foreign people"
**LOGOS:** "your blessings to an alien people"
**PNEUMA:** "your gifts over to a foreign people"
**Issue:** Greek ta sympheronta = the useful/profitable things. Theologically, these are the covenantal privileges of Israel (cf. Rom 3:1-2, 9:4-5). "Advantages" is most literal; "blessings" is most covenantal; "gifts" is more neutral. Consensus: "blessings" for its covenantal resonance.

---

## Disagreement 004 — v.5: "O memorial of Israel" vs. "O living memory of Israel"

**EMET:** "O memorial of Israel"
**LOGOS:** "O memorial of Israel"
**PNEUMA:** "You are the living memory of Israel"
**Issue:** Greek mnēmosynon Israēl = memorial/remembrance of Israel. PNEUMA adds "living" (not in the text). The address "memorial of Israel" positions the exiled people as the living repository of Israel's identity. Consensus: "O memorial of Israel."

---

## Disagreement 005 — v.6: "provoked God to anger" vs. "angered God"

**EMET:** "you provoked God to anger"
**LOGOS:** "you angered God"
**PNEUMA:** "you pushed God to anger"
**Issue:** Greek parōxynate ton theon = you provoked/irritated God. "Provoked to anger" is more literal and preserves the active causation. Consensus: "you angered God" — concise.

---

## Disagreement 006 — v.7: "your Maker" vs. "the one who made you"

**EMET:** "you provoked the one who made you"
**LOGOS:** "you provoked your Maker"
**PNEUMA:** "You provoked the one who made you"
**Issue:** Greek ton poiēsanta se = the one who made you. "Your Maker" (LOGOS) is more compact; "the one who made you" (EMET/PNEUMA) is more literal. Consensus: "your Maker" for concision.

---

## Disagreement 007 — v.8: "nourished you" and "nursed you"

**EMET:** "the eternal God who nourished you... Jerusalem who nursed you"
**LOGOS:** "the Eternal God who nourished you... Jerusalem who nursed you"
**PNEUMA:** "the Eternal God who fed you and raised you... Jerusalem, who nursed you like a mother"
**Issue:** PNEUMA adds "like a mother" (not in the Greek). Both verbs (trephō = nourish/nurse) are the same Greek root; the text uses repetition to draw the parallel between God and Jerusalem as nurturing figures. Consensus retains the distinction without the gloss.

---

## Disagreement 008 — v.9: Transition to Jerusalem's speech

**EMET:** "and she said: Listen, you neighbors of Zion!"
**LOGOS:** "and she said: Hear, you neighbors of Zion!"
**PNEUMA:** "and she spoke: Listen, you neighbors of Zion"
**Issue:** Greek legei = she says. Minor variation; "Hear" vs. "Listen." Consensus: "Hear" — more formal, appropriate for a public address.

---

## Disagreement 009 — v.12: "Let no one rejoice over me" vs. "Do not pity me"

**EMET:** "Let no one rejoice over me"
**LOGOS:** "Let no one rejoice over me"
**PNEUMA:** "Do not pity me"
**Issue:** PNEUMA mistranslates here. Greek mē tis epichairetō moi = let no one rejoice over me (epichairō = to rejoice at another's misfortune, schadenfreude). The prohibition is not about rejecting pity but about not gloating. EMET and LOGOS are correct. Consensus: "Let no one rejoice over me."

---

## Disagreement 010 — v.15: "aged" vs. "old man"

**EMET:** "had no respect for an old man and took no pity on a child"
**LOGOS:** "had no respect for the aged and no pity for the young"
**PNEUMA:** "had no respect for the elderly and no pity for children"
**Issue:** Greek presbutēs = old man/elder; nēpios = infant/young child. LOGOS and PNEUMA generalize appropriately. Consensus: "had no respect for the aged or pity for the young."

---

## Disagreement 011 — v.17: Question of helplessness

**EMET:** "But I, how can I help you?"
**LOGOS:** "But what can I do to help you?"
**PNEUMA:** "What can I do for you? There is nothing I can do."
**Issue:** PNEUMA adds "There is nothing I can do" (not in Greek). Greek ti gar dynēsomai boēthēsai hymin = how shall I be able to help you? The helplessness of the mother is expressed in the rhetorical question; adding a negative statement over-explains. Consensus: "But what can I do to help you?"

---

## Disagreement 012 — v.20: "petition" vs. "supplication" vs. "entreaty"

**EMET:** "the sackcloth of petition"
**LOGOS:** "the sackcloth of supplication"
**PNEUMA:** "sackcloth now, crying out"
**Issue:** Greek deēsis = supplication/petition. "Supplication" is more elevated; "petition" slightly more neutral. PNEUMA splits the image. Consensus: "sackcloth of supplication."

---

## Disagreement 013 — v.22: "eternal Savior" — capitalization and register

**EMET:** "your eternal savior"
**LOGOS:** "your eternal Savior"
**PNEUMA:** "the one who saves you forever"
**Issue:** Greek sōtēros aiōniou = of the eternal savior. Should "Savior" be capitalized? It refers to God. Consensus: capital S for consistency with other divine titles in the chapter.

---

## Disagreement 014 — v.23: "everlasting joy" vs. "eternal joy"

**EMET:** "with joy and gladness forever"
**LOGOS:** "with everlasting joy and gladness"
**PNEUMA:** "in joy and gladness that will never end"
**Issue:** Greek meta euphrosynēs aiōniou = with eternal/everlasting joy. EMET places "forever" at end of clause; LOGOS makes it an adjective. PNEUMA paraphrases. Consensus: "with everlasting joy and gladness."

---

## Disagreement 015 — v.24: "splendor of the Eternal" — compound phrase

**EMET:** "great glory and splendor of the Eternal"
**LOGOS:** "great glory and the splendor of the Eternal"
**PNEUMA:** "blazing with glory, radiant with the splendor of the Eternal"
**Issue:** PNEUMA adds "blazing" and "radiant" as intensifiers (not in the Greek). Greek doxē megale kai lampron tou aiōniou = great glory and splendor of the Eternal. Consensus: LOGOS with the added article "the."

---

## Disagreement 016 — v.26: "tender" vs. "delicate" vs. "soft"

**EMET:** "my tender children walked on rough paths"
**LOGOS:** "my delicate children have walked rough roads"
**PNEUMA:** "My tender children walked roads that were never meant for them"
**Issue:** Greek apaloi = soft/tender/delicate. Both "tender" and "delicate" work. PNEUMA adds "never meant for them" (interpretive expansion). Consensus: "my tender children."

---

## Disagreement 017 — v.28: "it was your will" vs. "it was your intention" vs. "you chose"

**EMET:** "it was your will to go astray from God"
**LOGOS:** "it was your intention to go astray"
**PNEUMA:** "You chose to wander from God"
**Issue:** Greek hōsper gar ēn hymin thymos = for just as was your will/spirit/desire. Greek thymos = passion/desire/will. "Chosen to wander" (PNEUMA) is more accessible. "It was your will" (EMET) is more literal. Consensus: "it was your will to go astray."

---

## Disagreement 018 — v.35: "inhabited by demons" vs. "demons will inhabit her"

**EMET:** "she will be inhabited by demons"
**LOGOS:** "demons will inhabit her"
**PNEUMA:** "a place haunted by demons"
**Issue:** Greek katoikēsousin en autē daimonia = demons will dwell in her. "Haunted" (PNEUMA) imports a ghost-story connotation. Consensus: "demons will inhabit her" — straightforward and preserves the eschatological echo of Isa 13:21.
